titulo: Práctica extra de Inglés — How Can We Reduce Household Waste?: vocabulario en situaciones nuevas, lectura de los gráficos, datos del texto y texto informativo vs. argumentativo

temas.nombre: Household Waste · Vocabulary in new situations
temas.explicacion:
Vocabulary — definiciones literales del libro (recuadros del glosario):
  • estimate — If you give an estimate, you give an amount or size that is not exact.
  • decay — When things decay, they slowly break down and rot.
Vocabulary — cómo lo usa el texto:
  • household — “Household waste includes all the trash created by the things we throw away.”
  • landfills — “When products are thrown away, they often end up in landfills. These are places where trash is buried in the ground.”
  • pollution — “You can help stop household waste pollution by following the three Rs: reduce, reuse, and recycle.”
  • litter — “Many household items end up as litter in parks, forests, rivers, lakes, and oceans.”
  • fines — “The city of Seattle, Washington passed a law in 2015. It requires people to recycle food waste. The city fines people who do not follow the law.”
  • composting — “You can also turn food and yard waste into dirt. This process is called composting.”
Ayuda (no es texto del libro): a fine = dinero que se paga como castigo por no cumplir una regla o ley; to fine = poner una multa. Litter = basura tirada donde no va. Pollution = lo que ensucia y daña la tierra, el agua o el aire.
temas.microleccion:
Ejemplo con OTRA palabra del texto (no es del temario): incinerators.
Paso 1 — buscá la pista en el texto: «Other trash items are burned in incinerators.» → son lugares donde se QUEMA la basura.
Paso 2 — pensá en una situación nueva: «The smoke came from a big building where the city burns trash.»
Paso 3 — escribí tu propia oración con la palabra: «Some cities burn their trash in incinerators.»
Paso 4 — revisá: empieza con mayúscula, tiene sujeto y verbo, termina con punto y la palabra tiene sentido en la oración.

temas.nombre: Household Waste · Reading the graphs: pie chart and bar graph
temas.explicacion:
Gráfico circular del libro (pie chart): AMERICAN WASTE (including recyclables)
  • paper products 27.4%
  • food waste 14.5%
  • plastics 12.7%
  • yard waste 10.5%
  • metal 8.9%
  • rubber, leather, and fabrics 8.7%
  • wood 6.9%
  • other 5.6%
  • glass 4.8%
Gráfico de barras del libro (bar graph): American Recycling Rates From 1960 to 2010 — eje vertical: PERCENT OF WASTE RECYCLED; eje horizontal: YEAR.
  • 1960: 6.4%
  • 1970: 6.6%
  • 1980: 9.6%
  • 1990: 16.0%
  • 2000: 28.5%
  • 2010: 34.0%
Ayuda para leer gráficos (no es texto del libro):
  • Primero leé el título: te dice de qué trata el gráfico.
  • En un pie chart cada parte es un pedazo del total (100%). La parte más grande es el número más grande.
  • En un bar graph la barra más alta es el número más grande. Leé el año abajo y el porcentaje arriba de la barra.
  • El gráfico es evidencia: sus números apoyan lo que dice el texto (por ejemplo, «Paper makes up more than one-quarter of the materials Americans throw away» → paper products 27.4%).
temas.microleccion:
Ejemplo con OTRO gráfico (inventado, no es del libro): «Bikes at our school» — 2021: 12 bikes · 2022: 18 bikes · 2023: 25 bikes.
Paso 1 — título: cuenta bicicletas por año.
Paso 2 — ¿qué año tiene la barra más alta? 2023 (25).
Paso 3 — ¿cuánto subió de 2022 a 2023? 25 − 18 = 7.
Paso 4 — conclusión en una oración: «More students came by bike every year.»
Para un pie chart: si «apples 30%» y «pears 20%», juntas son 30 + 20 = 50%, o sea la mitad (one-half).

temas.nombre: Household Waste · Comprehension: numbers, e-waste, recycling and solutions
temas.explicacion:
Párrafos literales del libro:

1 Household waste includes all the trash created by the things we throw away. And we throw away many things. In the United States, the average person throws away about 4.5 pounds (2 kilograms) of stuff every day. Only 1.5 pounds (0.7 kg) of that gets recycled or composted. The remaining 3 pounds (1.4 kg) is household waste.
2 What happens when you add up all the household waste Americans create? It comes out to about 164 million tons (149 metric tons) each year. But this is only an estimate from the US government. No one knows the exact amount of household waste Americans create. In fact, some experts believe it might be up to seven times that amount! In any case, a huge number of unwanted items end up in the garbage. And all of this garbage has serious effects on our environment.
5 Paper makes up more than one-quarter of the materials Americans throw away. Paper trash includes things such as notebooks and magazines. It also includes the cardboard and paper packages on the things we buy.
14 People are also finding ways to make better use of all our trash. For example, some clothing is made from recycled plastic bottles. Scientists are also studying whether a certain fungus can eat a common type of plastic. That would help cut back on all the plastic trash that fills up landfills.
24 Electronic waste, or e-waste, contains many toxic materials. But less than 15 percent of e-waste is recycled. That means most e-waste ends up in landfills or incinerators. When e-waste is buried or burned, the toxic materials can be released into the land, water, and air.
25 E-waste contains a high amount of lead. If e-waste is not disposed of properly, lead can leach into people’s water supplies. When people drink this water, it can damage their kidneys. It also damages their blood and their nervous systems.
30 The third most important step is recycle. When it is time to get rid of something, make every effort to recycle it rather than throwing it in the trash. In most areas, waste disposal companies provide separate recycling bins. So people can easily recycle paper, glass, and some kinds of plastic and metal. Some items, such as paint and batteries, are harder to recycle. But many areas have centers where these items can be brought for recycling.
31 Many places have laws that require people to recycle. The city of Austin, Texas has set a goal to cut the amount of trash it sends to landfills to nearly zero by the year 2040. The country of Sweden has nearly achieved this goal. It sends only 1 percent of its trash to landfills.

Pies de foto (captions) del libro:
  • “A woman in Seattle shows her three waste bins. Waste in the two large bins will be recycled. Waste in the small black bin will end up in a landfill.”
  • “Different types of plastic are given different numbers. Numbers 2, 4, and 5 are the least harmful to people and to the environment.”
  • “A worker moves shredded paper at a recycling center. Next, water will be added to the paper and it will be turned into pulp.”
  • “Americans recycle 71 percent of their steel cans. But they recycle only 50 percent of their aluminum cans.”

temas.nombre: Informational text vs. argumentative text: features and author’s purpose
temas.explicacion:
Informational text (texto informativo): gives facts and information to explain or teach about a topic. Features (características): headings (títulos de cada sección), photos with captions (pies de foto), charts and graphs (gráficos), numbers and facts (datos que se pueden comprobar), words in bold or highlighted with definitions (glosario).

Argumentative text (texto argumentativo): the author gives a claim (an opinion or position) and tries to persuade the reader to agree or take action. Features: a clear claim, reasons, evidence (facts and examples) that support the reasons, and a conclusion that repeats the claim or asks the reader to act. Often uses words like should, must, best, let’s.

Ejemplos de “How Can We Reduce Household Waste?”:
  • Heading: “Solutions to E-Waste Pollution”
  • Caption: “Take good care of your cell phone so it will last a long time.”
  • Glossary box: “decay — When things decay, they slowly break down and rot.”
  • Graph: “American Recycling Rates From 1960 to 2010”
  • Final paragraph: “Household waste is a major problem. But we have the power to solve it. And the solution begins with making smart choices in our everyday lives.”
Fact vs. opinion: a fact can be checked (proved true); an opinion tells what someone thinks or feels.
temas.microleccion:
Ejemplo con OTRO tema (no es del libro): agua.
Informativo: «A running tap uses about 6 liters of water per minute.» → solo da un dato que se puede comprobar; no nos pide nada.
Argumentativo, en 4 partes:
1) Claim: «Everyone should turn off the tap while brushing their teeth.»
2) Reason: «It saves a lot of clean water.»
3) Evidence: «A running tap uses about 6 liters of water per minute.»
4) Conclusion: «So, let’s close the tap and save water every day!»
Truco: si hay should / must / let’s y el autor quiere convencerte → argumentativo. Si solo explica con datos, títulos y gráficos → informativo.
